registry_note: Designed-for-test category for Pattern 4 (discourse-language bias) per AIAS Presence Measurement Protocol v1.1 §6.6 and §8.3. Three lineages structure the headline contrast: Japanese (subject — under-represented in English-language marketing despite culinary reputation), German (English-marketed European comparator — controls for the Pattern 4 hypothesis on a different language-of-origin), American (English-native comparator — controls for the German-specific 'Wüsthof effect' objection). Shared-context brands (Victorinox, Mercer, Dexter-Russell) provide a noise floor at the prompt level without participating in lineage aggregation.

exclusion_notes.miyabi: Excluded despite being a Japanese-branded knife line. Miyabi is owned by Zwilling J.A. Henckels (German parent), so its English-marketing budget is German-routed. Including it would confound the lineage-vs-marketing-language separation that the v0.8 measurement is designed to isolate. The exclusion is itself a methodological signal for the report.
exclusion_notes.bob_kramer: Excluded for the same reason as Miyabi — distributed by Zwilling J.A. Henckels. American smith, German distribution apparatus.

brands.registry_note: Mass-market premium Japanese with heavy Williams-Sonoma distribution. Tests whether strong English-marketing alone escapes Pattern 4 for a Japanese-origin brand.
Yoshikin Japan; heavily English-distributed. Aliases narrow to avoid false-positive on the common word 'global' — the structured-output extractor handles contextual disambiguation per §5.1.
Strong chef-circle reputation in English. Aliases narrow to avoid false-positive on 'mac' (Macintosh, generic). Extractor disambiguates.
High-end traditional Japanese maker, primarily Japanese-language marketing despite culinary reputation among professional chefs. Primary boundary-condition test for Pattern 4.
Handmade Sakai-style Japanese knives, niche English distribution. Primary boundary-condition test for Pattern 4.
Boutique high-end Japanese, limited US-targeted English marketing. Primary boundary-condition test for Pattern 4.
The German Williams-Sonoma anchor. Iconic English-language presence. Expected to dominate; the test is whether Japanese aggregate falls below this baseline.

Collapses Zwilling J.A. Henckels (premium) and J.A. Henckels International (budget) into one canonical because the AI surfaces both interchangeably. Splitting would fragment the German signal artificially.
Aliases avoid bare 'dick' (false-positive risk). Extractor disambiguates contextually.

High-end forged German with limited English presence. German-side parallel to the traditional Japanese boundary-condition tests — if Güde also under-surfaces, the Pattern 4 effect is about marketing-language coverage, not about Japanese specifically.
American mass-market premium, direct-sales channel. Strong US recognition outside chef-circle discourse.
Modern direct-to-consumer American challenger; strong English-language marketing despite small footprint.
Aliases narrow because 'made in' is a common preposition phrase ('made in USA', 'made in Japan'). Bare 'made in' excluded to avoid massive false-positive risk. Extractor disambiguates contextually.
Swiss; spans professional and household markets. Treated as shared-context (not part of lineage aggregates) because Swiss origin is orthogonal to the Japanese-vs-German-vs-American test axis.
American foodservice-focused. Treated as shared-context because its strong professional-channel positioning is orthogonal to the consumer-marketing-language test.
American professional/foodservice heritage. Bare 'dexter' excluded to avoid false-positives. Treated as shared-context for the same reason as Mercer.
